items.prose: An island has 3 red, 4 green and 8 blue lizards. When two of different colours meet, both turn the third colour.
items.question: Order the proof that they never all become one colour. Two lines may swap, and one does not belong.

lines.text: A meeting changes two counts by $-1$ and the third by $+2$.
So each difference between two counts changes by 0, 3 or $-3$.
So every difference keeps its remainder modulo 3.
At the start the differences are 1, 4 and 5: that is 1, 1 and 2 modulo 3.
One colour for all needs two counts of 0: a difference of 0.
So the lizards never all become one colour.
The total, 15, is odd, so the counts can never be made equal.
lines.why: The total never changes, and 15 of one colour also totals 15. The total proves nothing.

feedback.correct: Move, differences, modulo 3, the two values, conclusion.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Prove the invariant before you compare start and target.

byKey.d1: The total is the same at the start and at the target, so it rules nothing out.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the one about the total belongs.

explain.text: One meeting moves each difference by a multiple of 3, so the differences keep their remainders. The start has 1, 1 and 2 modulo 3, never 0, and one colour needs 0. Principle: compare the invariant at the start and at the target.

items.prose: A 7 × 7 board loses one square, and 16 straight 1 × 3 tiles must cover the other 48.

state.caption: Remove one square, then cover the rest with 16 straight 1 × 3 tiles.

items.question: Tap every square whose removal allows it.

feedback.correct: The nine squares $r_i c_j$ with $i, j \in \{1, 4, 7\}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Colour by $(i + j) \bmod 3$, then by $(i - j) \bmod 3$.

byKey.centre-only: The centre works, but so do eight other squares.
byKey.corners-only: The corners work, but so do five other squares.

explain.text: A straight tile covers one square of each class of $(i + j) \bmod 3$, and the classes hold 17, 16 and 16. So the removed square has $i + j \equiv 2$, and $(i - j) \bmod 3$ forces $i - j \equiv 0$ the same way. Exactly the nine squares with $i, j \in \{1, 4, 7\}$ pass both, and a search tiles each.

canvas.caption: The nine squares that both colourings allow.

items.prose: Points are placed inside an equilateral triangle of side 2, edges included.
items.question: What is the smallest number of points that always includes two at distance at most 1?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Cut the triangle into small triangles of side 1.

byKey.four: Four points can fail: the three corners and the centre are all more than 1 apart.
byKey.ten: Far fewer suffice: four small triangles are the boxes.

explain.text: Joining the midpoints cuts the triangle into four triangles of side 1, each of diameter 1. Five points put two in one small triangle. The corners and the centre fail, since the centre is $2/\sqrt{3} \approx 1.155$ from each corner.

items.prose: A fake coin may be heavier or lighter, and you must find it and say which, in three weighings.
items.question: Which can always be done? Select all that apply.

options.why: 26 cases fit under 27 outcomes, but no first weighing keeps every branch within 9.

options.text: 13 coins plus one coin known to be genuine
14 coins plus one coin known to be genuine
options.why: 14 coins give 28 cases, more than 27 outcomes.

feedback.correct: 12 coins, and 13 with a genuine coin.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count cases against 27 outcomes, then test the first weighing.

explain.text: Each coin is 2 cases, and three weighings give 27 outcomes, so 14 coins (28 cases) fail at once. Thirteen alone fail at the first weighing, but a genuine coin lets you weigh 5 against 4 plus it. A search of every plan confirms all four answers.

items.prose: Two ropes each burn for 120 minutes, unevenly. You have a lighter and nothing else.
items.question: Order the steps that measure 90 minutes. Two lines do not belong.

lines.text: Light rope A at both ends and rope B at one end, together.
Rope A goes out at 60 minutes.
At that moment, light the other end of rope B.
Rope B's last 60 minutes of burn now take 30.
Rope B goes out at 90 minutes.
Cut rope B into quarters and burn three of them.
lines.why: The burn is uneven, so a quarter of the length is not a quarter of the time.

lines.text: When A goes out, light a new rope at both ends.
lines.why: There is no third rope. Use what is left of rope B.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step waits for a rope to go out.

byKey.left-out: All five lines about ropes A and B belong.

explain.text: Rope A, lit at both ends, goes out at 60, when B has 60 minutes of burn left. A second flame on B halves that to 30, so B goes out at 90. Principle: a second flame halves the burn that is left.

items.prose: A tap, a 5-litre jug and an 11-litre jug. Each fill, empty or pour is one step.
items.question: What is the fewest steps that leaves 3 litres in a jug?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the states and search from the start, shortest first.

byKey.six: No route of 6 steps exists; a search of every state finds 12.
byKey.ten: No route of 10 steps exists; the shortest takes 12.
byKey.fourteen: That route works, but a shorter one takes 12.

explain.text: Pour fives into the 11 until it holds 10; the third five leaves 4 in the small jug. Empty the 11, pour the 4 in and add a five to make 9. The next five tops it up with 2 litres, leaving 3 after 12 steps, the fewest by search.

items.prose: A drawer holds 5 black, 3 white and 8 grey socks, and the light is off.
items.question: How many socks must you take to be sure of a matching pair that is not grey?

widget.label: Socks
widget.accept: 11: 8 grey, 1 black, 1 white, then one more

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Let the draw take every grey sock first.

byKey.four: Four socks guarantee a pair, but it could be grey.
byKey.ten: Ten can be all 8 grey, 1 black and 1 white.
byKey.nine: Nine can be 8 grey and 1 black.

explain.text: The worst case takes all 8 grey socks, then one black and one white: 10 socks and no usable pair. The eleventh is black or white and matches. Principle: the worst case spends every useless sock first.

items.question: Say the answer aloud, timing yourself, then open the model and tick the rubric.

widget.prompt: An interviewer asks why a 10 × 10 board cannot be covered by 25 straight 1 × 4 tiles. Say your answer aloud in under three minutes, then write the key lines. Give the colouring, the counts and the contradiction.
widget.model:
**Colour the board.** Give square $(i, j)$ the colour $(i + j) \bmod 4$. Number the colours 1 to 4 starting from the corner square, so colour 1 is $i + j \equiv 2$.

**What a tile covers.** A straight $1 \times 4$ tile lies along a row or a column. Its four squares have four consecutive values of $i + j$, so it covers one square of each colour.

**What 25 tiles cover.** Twenty-five tiles would cover exactly 25 squares of each colour.

**What the board has.** Counting each colour on the $10 \times 10$ board:

| Colour | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Squares | 25 | 26 | 25 | 24 |

**Contradiction.** Colour 2 has 26 squares and colour 4 has 24, but the tiles would cover 25 of each. So no tiling exists.

**Why area is no help.** The area, $100 = 25 \times 4$, allows a tiling, and a chessboard colouring balances at 50 and 50. Only the colouring that each tile meets once per colour decides it.

**Said aloud.** "Colour by $i + j$ modulo 4. Each straight tile covers one of each colour, so 25 tiles cover 25 of each. The board has 25, 26, 25 and 24. Contradiction, so it cannot be done."

rubric.text: Chooses a colouring that every tile meets once in each colour: $(i + j) \bmod 4$
States that each tile covers one square of each colour, so 25 tiles cover 25 of each
States the contradiction: 26 and 24 cannot both be 25
Notes that the area, $100 = 25 \times 4$, is no help
Says it in under three minutes, in order: colouring, counts, contradiction

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: The interviewer wants the colouring first, then the counts, then the contradiction. Saying why the area is no help shows you saw the trap.

items.title: Fifteen L pieces on a 6 by 10 board
items.question: Write the proof, then mark it against the model.

widget.prompt: An L-tetromino covers three squares in a line and one more square beside an end square, at right angles to the line. Pieces may be turned and flipped. Prove that fifteen of them cannot cover a 6 × 10 board, with no overlaps and no gaps. Give the reason for every line.
widget.model:
**Setting.** The board has 6 rows and 10 columns. A tiling places fifteen L pieces on it, each on four squares. Pieces may be turned or flipped, may not overlap and must cover every square.

**Area is no help.** The board has $6 \times 10 = 60$ squares, and fifteen pieces cover $15 \times 4 = 60$. So the proof must use the shape of the piece.

**The chessboard is no help.** Shade the board as a chessboard. The line of three covers two squares of its end shade and one of the other. The extra square touches an end, so it takes the other shade. Every L therefore covers 2 dark and 2 light, which the 30 and 30 board allows.

**Colour alternate columns.** Shade columns 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 dark and the even columns light. The board has 5 dark columns of 6 squares, so 30 dark and 30 light.

**Each L covers 3 of one colour and 1 of the other.** Turned or flipped, the line of three runs down one column or across three.

- *Down one column.* The line's three squares share a colour. The extra square lies in the next column, which has the other colour. So the split is 3 and 1.
- *Across three columns* $c$, $c + 1$, $c + 2$. Columns $c$ and $c + 2$ share a colour, so the line covers 2 of that colour and 1 of the other. The extra square sits at right angles to the line, above or below an end, so it is in column $c$ or $c + 2$. So the split is 3 and 1.

**Track dark minus light.** By the last step each piece adds $+2$ or $-2$ to the number of dark squares covered minus light. Say $a$ pieces add $+2$ and $15 - a$ add $-2$. The total is

$$2a - 2(15 - a) = 4a - 30.$$

This is never 0, because 30 is not a multiple of 4. The nearest it comes is $\pm 2$, at $a = 7$ or $a = 8$.

**Contradiction.** A tiling covers every square exactly once. So it covers all 30 dark and all 30 light, and dark minus light is $30 - 30 = 0$. The pieces cannot total 0, so no tiling exists.

**Rows work too.** Alternate rows give the same 3 and 1 split and the same 30 and 30, so either stripe proves it.

rubric.text: Shows that area and the chessboard decide nothing: $60 = 15 \times 4$, and on a chessboard each L covers 2 dark and 2 light
Colours alternate columns (or rows) and counts the board: 30 of each colour
Tick only if both cases are argued: proves that every L covers 3 of one colour and 1 of the other, with the line of three along one stripe and across three stripes
Tick only if both are given: each piece changes dark minus light by $\pm 2$, and fifteen such changes total $4a - 30$, never 0, against the 0 the board needs

feedback.correct: Compare your proof with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: The chessboard balances every L, so you needed a colouring that each L meets unevenly. Stripes give a split of 3 and 1 in every position. Fifteen steps of $\pm 2$ cannot cancel, yet the board needs them to.
